meta.title: The C Form: The Shape Does Not Slide
meta.summary: Flattening the C form's thirds forces two fingers to swap places and drops a third note out of the window entirely, so the minor grip is not the major grip with one finger moved back.

spans.text: Three of those seven dots aren't in the grip at all —
. And here's the number that makes the edge effect real rather than abstract: A major's C form window holds eight dots, A minor's holds seven — the only one of the five that ends up with
dots in minor than in major.
There's a practical payoff to all this rearranging, and it's the point of the lesson. In major, the compact triad here is strings 3-2-1 at frets
. In minor that fragment doesn't exist, because the note on string 1 left the window. What you take instead is strings 4-3-2 at frets
. Three adjacent strings, nothing to stretch for, and it's the shape most players actually reach for out of this form.

This is where the C form lives: frets

. Nobody bars this form whole in either quality; in minor it isn't even a candidate — the root would be stranded past a full barre's reach.

That's the real lesson under the fingering shuffle. "The minor form is the major form with one finger moved back" turns out to be true of three of the five grips in this chapter — the next one is the cleanest of them, with a single string carrying the entire change. It's false here. Two fingers swap places, a whole string disappears from the grip, and the fragment you end up playing lives on a different set of strings altogether. Chapter order put the C form first on purpose: it's where that easy intuition breaks before it has a chance to calcify.
